newsitem.title: USA: President of troubled Maine Yankee resigns.
newsitem.headline: President of troubled Maine Yankee resigns.

text.p: Maine Yankee president Charles Frizzle resigned Friday in the first step of a management reorganization of the troubled nuclear power facility, the plant's directors announced.

Frizzle agreed to step down following a series of unscheduled shutdowns by the 24-year-old plant in Wiscasset and a critical regulatory review that said management had fostered a work environment that placed cost concerns before those of safety.

"(The board) decided that Maine Yankee needs new leadership to deal with deep-rooted cultural issues, a changing regulatory environment and unprecedented financial pressures," said David Flanagan, president of Maine Yankee's board of directors.

Flanagan, chief executive officer of Maine Central Maine Power said that a broad restructing of Maine Yankee's management was being considered and that additional changes would likely be announced in early 1997.

Flanagan said the utilities would spend an additional $30 million on maintainence in 1997 and $7 million on capital projects after a special NRC inspection that found a variety of equipment problems and criticized Maine Yankee management.
Among the ideas the board was considering is a proposal that management of all of the independently operated nuclear plants in New England be consolidated under a single corporation, Flanagan said.

The 910-megawatt Maine Yankee plant has been forced to go off-line repeatedly for the past two years because of equipment problems problem ranging from cracked steam tubes to missing wires in key reactor safety systems.

The plant's latest outage began Dec. 6 when engineers discovered several control room electical cables were improperly installed. The plant may not return to operation until early February, spokeswoman Maureen Brown said Friday.

The inspection was requested by Gov. Angus King after an NRC investigation raised questions about whether Maine Yankee's emergency core cooling system was properly licensed during a power upgrade in the late 1980s.
The Justice Department is also investigating allegations that Maine Yankee misled the NRC about the adequacy of a computer code used to test the systen. The plant has denied wrongdoing.

The plant has been restricted to 90 percent capacity while a new computor test is eing reveiwed. Gov. King has said he thinks it is unlikely the plant will be allowed to return to 100 percent capacity.

Frizzle, who has held his post since 1989, will remain with the company until a successor is selected in early 1997. The board wants the next president to be from outside of New England and "a bigger organization," Flanagan told reporters.

Maine Yankee is 38 percent owned by Central Maine Power Co, 20 percent each by New England Electric System and Northeast Utilities, seven percent by Bangor Hydro, five percent by Maine Public Service Co. and 10 percent by other New England utilities.
